messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette failed validation. Make ONLY the targeted changes listed below.

Previous vignette:
Liam, a 56-year-old detective of Oceania background, came to treatment after years of carrying a childhood that still seemed to sit inside every shift and every quiet moment at home. He described being raised by a caregiver whose physical abuse was sudden, humiliating, and impossible to predict: the smell of something burnt in the kitchen would sometimes be the only warning before a blow, and even now that same acrid scent could pull him back without preparation to the cramped rooms, the heat, and the fear of waiting for what came next. He had learned to scan people quickly, especially those who looked like the men who had hurt him in childhood, and to mistrust even small flashes of warmth or ease. What unsettled him most was that positive emotion itself could feel dangerous, as if a rare moment of relief was the moment before something terrible happened. When he tried to talk about what had happened, he often lost the thread entirely and could not finish the story, and he would come away feeling that his own reactions proved he was a lousy coper and that there must be something fundamentally wrong with the kind of person he was. Over time, those beliefs had hardened into a conviction that the world did not operate by any rules he could trust; it had, in his words, “completely broken” the way he thought life was supposed to work.

Those meanings fed his memory in painful ways. When Liam tried to explain the abuse, the account would fragment, and the more he struggled to tell it in order, the more his mind would snap to vivid, uninvited scenes: a hand raised, the stale heat of the room, the burnt smell hanging in the air. The recollection was not distant or narrative in shape; it arrived with the force of something happening again, and with it came intense rage that made his jaw clench and his chest tighten. He said that the memory could be triggered instantly by something in his surroundings, as though his mind had learned to stand ready for a return of the old danger. At work, in the station or out on a scene, if he caught even a faint burnt odor from wiring, a kitchen fire, or scorched material, he would be thrown back into the abuse before he had time to think. If someone in the street or in a file photo resembled one of the victims he had seen over the years, he would feel the memory sharpen again, not only of the childhood assaults but of his own powerlessness in the face of them. His belief that his world had been shattered, and that he himself had somehow invited the treatment, kept the memories bound to shame and anger rather than history. The more he blamed himself, the more the scenes seemed to confirm that he had been weak all along, and the more he tried to explain, the less coherent the story became.

To manage this, Liam narrowed his life. He avoided other people whenever he could, ate lunch alone, and found reasons not to linger after work. He had even started avoiding clothes that resembled what he had worn at certain times in childhood, because the wrong shirt could make him feel exposed and stranded in an old role he hated. At the same time, pulling away from people and from the memories gave the recollections more room to intrude. When he detached himself from them, they returned less as something observed than as something that broke through abruptly, and that unpredictability made him even more alert. He remained superalert at home and on duty, having difficulty falling asleep because he needed to stay watchful, and he noticed that his body reacted strongly whenever something reminded him of the abuse. He would jolt at small sounds, pace the house, and keep checking the door or the stove, as though the next threat might be waiting in the ordinary details of the room. That constant guardedness made it easier for the burnt smell, the sight of a similar face, or even a burst of unexpected happiness to catch him unprepared, and each fresh reminder seemed to confirm his conviction that the world could turn instantly. The more he withdrew and monitored for danger, the more isolated and self-critical he became, certain that these were the failures of a man who had not coped well enough and who could never quite keep himself safe.

By the time he sought help, the cycle had begun to cost him his marriage, his sleep, and his confidence at work. He was still functioning as a detective, but he was exhausted by the effort of staying on guard and frightened that one wrong smell or one unexpected moment of feeling good would throw him back into the old scenes in front of colleagues or suspects. What brought him in was the sense that the life he had built around vigilance was shrinking, and that he was becoming more cut off from everyone he cared about. He said he wanted relief, but what he feared most was that the memories would keep arriving without warning and prove, once again, that he was not someone who could ever truly withstand them.

Issues to fix:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette shows reminders leading to avoidance or hypervigilance, but it does not clearly state that triggers themselves drive Liam’s maladaptive strategies in a causal way within one paragraph.
  e.g. "She stopped taking that route to work entirely — better to add twenty minutes to her commute than to feel that way again."
  e.g. "When the anniversary came around, she kept herself moving all day, cleaning, cooking, anything, because sitting still meant the thoughts would catch up."
  e.g. "She started leaving events early, telling herself she was tired, because staying too long meant the chances of something going wrong only multiplied."
- Triggers → Memory: The vignette states that a burnt smell and similar faces cue the memory, but it does not clearly present triggers as causing the traumatic memory in the required causal direction.
  e.g. "The smell of his cologne in the lift sent the whole night flooding back before she had even reached her floor."
  e.g. "Hearing that song on the radio dragged her straight back into the room where it happened, as if no time had passed at all."
  e.g. "Walking past the bus stop where it occurred, she was no longer on the street — she was back there, every detail sharp and close."
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: The vignette says self-blaming beliefs keep the memories bound to shame, but it does not explicitly show negative appraisals driving the traumatic memory itself in a causal sequence.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette shows the memory being triggered by surroundings, but it does not explicitly state that the memory then leads to new triggers or increased triggering stimuli.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: The vignette describes threat feelings increasing self-criticism, but it does not clearly show a sense of threat producing negative appraisals in the required causal relationship.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Memory: The vignette shows avoidance and monitoring making him more alert and vulnerable to reminders, but it does not clearly state that maladaptive strategies cause the memory to recur in a causal way.
  e.g. "She had been avoiding any mention of it for so long that when the memory finally surfaced, it was louder than it had ever been — all that suppression had kept it fresh."
  e.g. "Not talking about it meant the memory had never been put anywhere; it remained in her, undisturbed and intact, exactly where she had left it."
  e.g. "The effort of keeping it at a distance had paradoxically kept it close — she had thought about not thinking about it every day for three years."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals: The vignette shows withdrawal increasing self-criticism, but it does not clearly state that maladaptive strategies lead to negative appraisals in the required causal relationship.
  e.g. "Three years of avoiding it had told her something she couldn't easily argue with: that she must be more fragile than other people, or she would have been over this by now."
  e.g. "Each time she used a safety behaviour to get through the day, she felt the quiet accumulation of evidence that she couldn't cope without it."
  e.g. "The fact that she still needed to do all of this — the checking, the planning, the long way round — confirmed, in some wordless way, that she wasn't getting better."

---

Return ONLY patch blocks — do NOT return the full vignette.

For each REQUIRED EDGE MISSING — produce one INSERT_AFTER block.
Find a paragraph in the vignette that already mentions component A, and add a sentence
after it that shows A influencing B through natural clinical language.
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
[copy 1–2 sentences from the vignette — the anchor after which to insert]
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
[one or two sentences that convey A influencing B, written as natural clinical prose]
<<<END>>>

Output ONLY these patch blocks. No prose, no explanation, no full vignette.

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
He described being raised by a caregiver whose physical abuse was sudden, humiliating, and impossible to predict: the smell of something burnt in the kitchen would sometimes be the only warning before a blow, and even now that same acrid scent could pull him back without preparation to the cramped rooms, the heat, and the fear of waiting for what came next. He had learned to scan people quickly, especially those who looked like the men who had hurt him in childhood, and to mistrust even small flashes of warmth or ease.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
When that burnt smell came up at work or on the street, Liam would stop what he was doing, move away from people, and keep checking the room until he felt he had some control again; the reminder itself drove the avoidance and the constant watchfulness. It was easier to add distance than to risk being caught off guard by it again.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
He described being raised by a caregiver whose physical abuse was sudden, humiliating, and impossible to predict: the smell of something burnt in the kitchen would sometimes be the only warning before a blow, and even now that same acrid scent could pull him back without preparation to the cramped rooms, the heat, and the fear of waiting for what came next. He had learned to scan people quickly, especially those who looked like the men who had hurt him in childhood, and to mistrust even small flashes of warmth or ease.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
The smell did not just remind him of the abuse; it would drag him straight back into one of those childhood rooms, so vividly that for a moment he was no longer in the present at all. A burnt pan at home or scorched wiring at the station could do it before he had time to steady himself.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
What unsettled him most was that positive emotion itself could feel dangerous, as if a rare moment of relief was the moment before something terrible happened. When he tried to talk about what had happened, he often lost the thread entirely and could not finish the story, and he would come away feeling that his own reactions proved he was a lousy coper and that there must be something fundamentally wrong with the kind of person he was.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
The more he told himself that he should have handled it better, the more the memory seemed to come forward on its own, as if his mind kept returning him to the scene to prove the point he feared was true. His self-blame made the abuse feel less like something that had happened to him and more like evidence that he was weak.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
The recollection was not distant or narrative in shape; it arrived with the force of something happening again, and with it came intense rage that made his jaw clench and his chest tighten. He said that the memory could be triggered instantly by something in his surroundings, as though his mind had learned to stand ready for a return of the old danger.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Once it had burst back like that, he started noticing possible warnings everywhere — the whine of wiring, the smell of a kitchen gone too hot, the hard set of a stranger’s face. After the memory had flooded him, ordinary details began to look like they might be the next sign of trouble.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
At work, in the station or out on a scene, if he caught even a faint burnt odor from wiring, a kitchen fire, or scorched material, he would be thrown back into the abuse before he had time to think. If someone in the street or in a file photo resembled one of the victims he had seen over the years, he would feel the memory sharpen again, not only of the childhood assaults but of his own powerlessness in the face of them.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Feeling that danger so constantly made his view of himself harsher, and he came to take it as proof that his life had been altered in some permanent way. The threat he felt every day quietly confirmed his belief that he was not the kind of man who got to feel safe.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
To manage this, Liam narrowed his life. He avoided other people whenever he could, ate lunch alone, and found reasons not to linger after work. He had even started avoiding clothes that resembled what he had worn at certain times in childhood, because the wrong shirt could make him feel exposed and stranded in an old role he hated.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
The more he kept the experience at a distance, the less it seemed to stay put; weeks of not talking about it left the memory intact and raw, so that when it did surface it came back with a force that felt fresh. What he had thought would keep him safe had, in practice, kept the scene close to hand.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
At the same time, pulling away from people and from the memories gave the recollections more room to intrude. When he detached himself from them, they returned less as something observed than as something that broke through abruptly, and that unpredictability made him even more alert.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Each time he chose to leave early, sit apart, or keep his distance, the decision carried its own quiet message: that he needed those precautions because he could not simply cope like other people. Over time, those habits became another source of the belief that he was fragile and permanently behind everyone else.
<<<END>>>
